claims.claim: Reviewers experience long shader compilation times when starting the game.

citations.review_text: Bro.   What’s the deal with the hour long shader compile at the start of game?

The optimization is completely unacceptable for a game with such a simplistic art style. Waiting 20 minutes for shaders to compile, only to step outside and watch the FPS counter collapse, genuinely felt like a slap in the face.

From what I understand, this game has been in Early Access for years, yet there doesn't seem to have been any effort put into improving performance.

Compiling shaders for 2 hours.

Fix your game

claims.claim: This cohort reports poor optimization and inconsistent frame rates, with frame drops occurring even on high-end hardware and low graphical settings.

citations.review_text: The game is good and fun, but the optimization is crap, I'm getting 50 fps with graphics set to "Balanced" and DLSS "Balanced" enabled, on an offline server with zero structures built by me. It's frustrating, considering I can play Crimson Desert with everything on high at 80–100 fps.

It would be pretty nice if the game ran smoother in a consistent way. It's pretty disappointing and distracting to have so much stuttering during gameplay. 

And is not a matter of power. With a 7800x3d(upgraded recently but haven't updated the steam specs yet) and a rtx4080, 32GB of ddr5 ram, this game should be a breeze.

Also, and this is a personal thing, the position of the camera in-game feels very awkward.

I'd also suggest the on onboarding experience got more work, it feels very sluggish compared to other initial experiences in the genre, like Runscpe DW, I feel like they solved this problem a little better, helping the player to learn the ropes in a more intentional way, through more precise goals.

Those are my 2 cents. I look forward to the full game where I hope all of this is addressed. For now, I wouldn't recommend it yet.

Its literally unplayable. i tried every option available and it even spikes in performance mode with every option turned on low or off. The gameplay itself seems fine! i love the graphics (from what i was able to see so far)

I played Enshrouded because I really liked the game's concept, but optimization remains one of the worst aspects of the experience.

The main problem is that the performance simply does not match the visuals being delivered. The game demands too much from both the GPU and CPU for a graphical result that, in my opinion, does not justify such a heavy hardware load.

What bothers me the most is the main menu. It makes no sense for a menu to consume so many resources. In many games, GPU usage drops or is limited on this screen, but in Enshrouded the exact opposite happens. My graphics card jumps to nearly 100% usage, the fans speed up, and temperatures rise dramatically.

In my case, the GPU hotspot has already exceeded 100°C while just sitting in the game menu. This is something I have never seen happen in several other titles that are far more visually impressive. A menu should not be putting hardware under that level of load.

The character creation screen also urgently needs optimization. It is another moment where the game seems to consume resources excessively without any real necessity. There is no justification for a character creator to require so much processing power.

During gameplay, I also experienced FPS drops, stuttering, and inconsistent performance. What is most frustrating is that lowering graphical settings does not always bring a significant improvement, creating the impression that there are deeper issues within the engine.

I am not criticizing the game's content. The building system is excellent, the world is interesting, and there is a lot of potential here. My criticism is exclusively about the technical side.

Keen Games needs to prioritize optimization. And I am not talking only about small adjustments. The game needs major optimization work, especially in the main menu and character creation screen, where resource consumption becomes absurd.

Enshrouded just feels incredibly flat. Very little of what you do feels meaningful, and the progression system never really gives you that satisfying sense of achievement. You're constantly unlocking new crafting recipes and materials, but most of it feels like busywork rather than genuine progression.

Combat is probably my biggest disappointment. Almost every encounter boils down to spamming attack, blocking occasionally, and repeating until everything is dead. There's very little skill expression or depth, and the higher-level MMO-style enemies just turn fights into longer, less enjoyable versions of the same thing.

There are very few enemy variations to keep things interesting, and once you've explored one section, you've largely seen everything it has to offer. Dying in the Shroud is especially frustrating because it turns the already tedious corpse run into an even bigger chore.

Exploration starts off exciting, but quickly becomes tedious. Reaching quest markers often means long runs through areas that massively out-level you, so it frequently devolves into repeated death runs just to reach your destination. Once you get there, you're usually rewarded with another repetitive dungeon or a handful of crafting materials that don't feel particularly exciting.

Traversal is another weak point. The glider is fun at first, but movement overall feels overly floaty, and the extreme verticality of the world often makes getting around more frustrating than enjoyable.

I appreciate that Enshrouded tries to do something different from other survival games, but it ends up feeling like a collection of me…

Meh

Bought to play with a friend and wish I had refunded it. While I definitely am not someone who enjoys these type of games to begin with, Enshrouded also didn't seem particularly outstanding for lovers of the genre. 

It looks alright. Not spectacular, but like a lovingly made indie game. The gameplay itself is ... fine but not polished or particularly fun. The animations look uninspired, the combat is uninspired, the rest of the gameplay is uninspired.

It's serviceable and if you really, really need another base building + crop farming game, this might bring some relief. But if you're not a sucker for doing the same ♥♥♥♥ you already did in all those other games - at a quality that simply isn't doing anything that other games aren't doing better - there are just better games to play. Nothing I did in my ~7 hours of playing struck me as particularly interesting or well made. 

It does what it does and I guess for some people that's all that's needed to have fun. But I can find dozens of games that do these things better or in a more interesting way and given how much these games waste on mundane tasks, I believe you can only play so many of them with the time you have available in your life. So I'd say go for a better one, can't be that hard to top this bland gameplay.

Lots of potential, but...

There's a lot of basic stuff that's either implemented poorly or missing.
Combat feels weightless, movement is floaty and clunky at the same time. Not sure if this is intended or if changes are planned.

Building system is so full of potential, but with lots of annoying quirks like not having drag-to-build or logical surface snapping. Blocks seem to snap to an awkward "world grid" instead of each other.

My buddy baited me to get this game, I got it and I regret it so much. My main issues are the unsatisfactory combat, having to wait 10 minutes each time I load the game up so I don't get 2 frames while paying it, the boring variety of enemies, and the progression is super slow. To me this game just does not feel special. I tried to give this game multiple chances and I regretted it each time.

Cool moments and ideas, but I'm forced to grind and work to be able to enjoy the fun part - not what I look for in a game. Combat is super janky and not very deep or fun in itself. If you are big into collecting resources, crafting and building you might like it more. I don't think the game is well-balanced between the one half of it that is a chill building survival game and the other half that is a fantasy dungeon-raiding game. I see the vision but the moment-to-moment is not where it needs to be.

Took three ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hours to compile shaders so i'm outside of the refund window. Figured I might as well give it a full shot and wow, This game is pure unwashed ass. Exactly how many times should i expect to have to hit dodge before i'm 2 shot by a same level wolf on easy difficulty? Why do enemies never seem  to stagger no matter what i attack with but they will attack me in the middle of my attack animations and knock me out of it?

This feel like a slightly prettier valheim and that game is terrible too.

Game controls and menus are all designed for controller gameplay. Makes it a nightmare if you are using Keyboard and mouse tbh.

The building menu is overcomplicated and needs an absurd amount of resources for you to actually build anything decent.

Honestly wouldn't recommend unless you enjoy games with a STEEP grind.

The constant need to manage your stamina for everything and lack of significant stamina related upgrades is frutrating too.

citations.review_text: Was hoping this could be a fun game for my friends and I to play together, but the forced shared progression really ruins it for us. How about I just go and play Valheim instead

It is a nice game, but this problem makes it borderline, as everytime i want to spin it up, it needs to build the shaders first...

I hope the devs get this massive issue fixed. For me it seems to be over, as I can't play the game anymore :(

I have 3-4 hours of free time per day TOPS to play something. I don't even play games daily sometimes, so when I do play something, it's supposed to be at least somewhat meaningful.
This game is frustrating.
The map feels like the game wants to give you a climbing option, yet you have none.
The combat has potential, but it's full of shortcomings even with the last update as of the time of the review.
The graphics and the performance is god-awful and is lacking despite the game having textures of inconsistent quality and the only good thing is the shading and the lighting (which is probably the main cause of performance being bad).
The game's progression system is awkward and unintuitive. You have a ton of different work stations, a ton of quests to upgrade them, yet you don't feel like you accomplish something. You just feel like nothing's changed.
The gear progression is even more awkward. Yeah, okay, I can craft armor. But why can't I craft weapons then? Why should I search for weapons Fortnite-style and "upgrade" them with coins and whatnot?
Sometimes I feel like asking "why can't you just be normal?" but even if I ask this I understand that there will be no answer.
The game is full of what-ifs and if-onlys. 
But what I get is another shader loading downtime.
Every update released forces the game's shaders to reset, which in turn forces your PC to reload them, which takes about 20-30 minutes on a decent PC (specs included in the review). 
Do I feel like wasting half an hour waiting for the game to load half it's graphics? I am playing as a mage, I literally can neither see my attacks nor the parry signals from enemies before the shaders've finished compiling. But after those 20-30 minutes I'm already super-tired of the game and I just quit it.

Game's specific mechanics aside, it objectively needs two things:
A climbing mechanic
A performance overhaul

Until then, consider that you won't be able to see a 'Recommend' review until your shaders finish compiling.

claims.claim: Reviewers praise the voxel building system, stating it offers extensive freedom and detailed crafting for structures.

citations.review_text: This game is great!  I would recommend it to anyone who enjoys this genre.  There is so many things to do a items to build and upgrade.  The build mechanics are some of the best I have used so it is really fun to build elaborate structures.

We have reached the grand finale of my Co-op Trilogy. After suffering respiratory collapse in Valheim and developing severe poultry induced schizophrenia in R.E.P.O I bring you Enshrouded (42.3 hours on record) This Early Access purgatory features one of the most advanced voxel building systems on the market, which tragically triggered my professional deformation as a former real estate agent.

Let me be professionally clear: the zoning laws in this game are an absolute joke. You are given the tools to build a magnificent, brick by brick architectural masterpiece, but the developers force you to construct it directly above the "Shroud" a swirling, highly toxic, metaphysical cancer that dissolves human lungs in four minutes.

Do you know how hard it is to sell this kind of property? I have to mentally pitch these ruins to imaginary clients just to cope with the gameplay. "Welcome to this charming, rustic fixer upper! It boasts an open concept floor plan, zero neighbors, and is situated in a highly lucrative, whisper quiet neighborhood featuring a panoramic view of absolute, agonizing death. Please do not open the basement door, sir, or the radioactive fog will consume your physical form. But just think of the property tax savings!" From a market value perspective, building a homestead here is financial and literal suicide.

Then, there is the sociological anomaly known as my friend Denis. Denis initially refused to play this game because there was no water. He boycotted the entire Early Access title over a lack of H2O. So, the developers eventually added water. Denis logged in, stared at the newly implemented water, and immediately complained that the game "lacks the atmosphere of Valheim."

Of course it lacks the atmosphere of Valheim, Denis! Enshrouded actually has a living world, quests, and things to do. Valheim’s "atmosphere" consists of standing perfectly still in an empty, depressing Swedish forest, wheezing from asthma, waiting for your own roof to cave in an…

52 hours in and I feel like I've barely scratched the surface.

This is the first survival-crafting game in a long time that doesn't just throw you into a sandbox and tell you to "make your own fun." Every time I think I'm heading toward my next objective, I get distracted by a cave, a ruined city, a hidden chest, a new NPC, or another piece of gear. The world constantly rewards exploration.

The building system is honestly the best I've ever used. It's incredibly flexible without becoming frustrating, and the voxel system lets you create almost anything you can imagine. Building a cozy farmhouse one day and a castle carved into a mountainside the next never gets old.

The progression is what really hooked me. Quests unlock new crafters, new stations, new building pieces, farming, and new ways to explore instead of simply handing you bigger numbers. It always feels like you're working toward something meaningful.

It's not perfect. Combat is good, but I wish there were more enemy variety, and I still hope one day we'll be able to permanently reclaim areas from the Shroud. Those are really my biggest complaints
Honestly I love this game more than Valheim. I just enjoy the building a lot more. I love that its a manmade world because it doesn't feel so empty. I love repairing old villages to make my home
One of, if not the best survival builder out there. Huge world to explore. Arguably the best builder in the genre. Decent combat. Really solid game.

A dream game for anyone who loves both Minecraft and Terraria. It combines Terraria's epic fantasy world design with a building system that gives you far more freedom than Minecraft. You're not limited to simple blocks, you can customize structures piece by piece and build almost anything you can imagine.

The gameplay loop can get repetitive after a while: explore a new region, gather resources, craft better gear, and repeat. Playing with friends helps a lot and makes the grind much more enjoyable.

My only real complaint is the optimization. Despite being able to run games like Crimson Desert, Black Myth: Wukong, and Expedition 33 at a stable 60 FPS, Enshrouded struggles to maintain 60 FPS even on the lowest settings with upscaling enabled. Hopefully this gets improved before full release, since the game is still in Early Access.

Overall, it's a fantastic survival-crafting game with one of the best building systems out there.

Overall the game can be really fun and engaging. The world is large and interesting with lots to explore. Building is fantastic, the voxel system is amazing. Generally speaking the game is great. 

Except, it's extremely clunky and feels like a lot of the designs were put in place solely to be infuriating.

First, the positives: the world is gorgeous. It feels enormous, varied and thoughtfully handcrafted without feeling built around quest markers. I constantly see something in the distance and think, “Can I actually get over there?” Usually, the answer is yes. 

The voxel terrain might be my favorite part. Mining through mountains, excavating tunnels and creating alternate entrances is fantastic, especially because the results can look surprisingly natural. Combined with building, verticality and gliding, Enshrouded offers environmental interaction I haven’t experienced elsewhere. 

I’d also love a free-use grappling hook on natural terrain. I understand restricting it inside Spires, dungeons and puzzles to prevent bypassing designed routes. But let it attach to ordinary destructible rock with reasonable range/stamina limits. Falling off a cliff shouldn’t always mean walking around a mountain or mining a staircase through it. 

Exploration itself is fantastic. Around level 13-15, I was already wearing roughly level-30 gear because I pushed into areas I had absolutely no business being in and survived long enough to loot them. 

I LOVE that.

Some call it the best survival game, others the best action RPG. Few games have left me as conflicted as Enshrouded.
Don't get me wrong, Enshrouded has genuine qualities. But it also carries a weight of frustrations and missed opportunities that are hard to ignore.

- Combat : Souls-Inspired But Poorly Executed
The combat system clearly draws inspiration from souls-likes, but feels unfinished and archaic even after the recent combat update.
Melee is at a severe disadvantage compared to ranged, not just in power, but how it feels. Every action, whether attacking or dodging, locks you into a 0.5+ second animation with no way to cancel. Getting surrounded by three enemies means getting infinitely staggered while your own attacks don't stagger them at all.
The parry window is too lenient, you can parry on the very first frame and it always works, which makes it feel cheap rather than satisfying. The dodge on the other hand feels half-broken, with i-frames that seem to exist on paper only, you'll take damage mid-roll constantly.
Heavy attacks hitting only a single target even when enemies are standing side by side is baffling. The camlock takes ages to reorient when an enemy moves behind you. Enemy AI is inconsistent, some won't detect you standing right in front of them, even hitting them while others get stuck in walls and fall through the floor when hit.
Daggers are arguably the worst offender, weak, with a single animation, and stealth as a playstyle is essentially non-existent.
Ranged combat avoids most of these issues but becomes incredibly monotonous, you'll repeat the exact same actions for dozens of hours with no variation. This was a major complaint at launch and unfortunately remains unchanged.
